subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.stem: Which structures are found in all cells, both prokaryotic and eukaryotic?
choices: Nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes and a cell wall
Plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA and ribosomes
Plasma membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm and chloroplasts
Cell wall, plasmids, 80S ribosomes and a nucleoid
items.note: Every cell has a membrane, cytoplasm (mostly water), DNA as genetic material and ribosomes. Nuclei and mitochondria are eukaryote-only; walls are not universal.

items.stem: A drawing of a mitochondrion is 45 mm long. The mitochondrion is actually 3 µm long. What is the magnification of the drawing?
items.note: Convert to the same unit first: 45 mm = 45 000 µm. Magnification = image ÷ actual = 45 000 ÷ 3 = 15 000. The usual error is forgetting to convert mm to µm.

items.stem: Which feature is found in a Gram-positive bacterium such as Bacillus but not in an animal cell?
choices: A plasma membrane made of phospholipids
Ribosomes that make proteins in the cytoplasm
DNA that carries the genetic information
A cell wall made of peptidoglycan
items.note: Prokaryotes have a peptidoglycan wall, a nucleoid (naked DNA), 70S ribosomes and often plasmids. Membranes, ribosomes and DNA are shared by all cells.

items.stem: A micrograph shows a cell with a cell wall, a large central vacuole and no chloroplasts. The cell is most likely:
choices: A fungal hypha cell
An animal liver cell
A plant root cell
A Gram-positive bacterium
items.note: A wall plus a large central vacuole is the typical plant pattern; root cells receive no light, so they have no chloroplasts. Animal cells have no wall; bacteria have no large central vacuole.

items.stem: Which statement about red blood cells in mammals makes them an atypical cell?
choices: They contain many nuclei because they form by cells fusing together
They have a thin cell wall that stops them bursting in the blood plasma
They lack a nucleus when mature, which leaves more room for haemoglobin
They lack a plasma membrane, so haemoglobin is free in the blood
items.note: Mature mammalian erythrocytes have no nucleus (and no mitochondria). Multinucleate = skeletal muscle fibres; no cell has no membrane.

items.stem: Skeletal muscle fibres are described as atypical because they:
choices: Contain no nucleus at maturity and rely on companion cells
Contain many nuclei and are much longer than a typical cell
Lack mitochondria and depend on anaerobic respiration only
Are joined end to end into one tube with sieve plates between them
items.note: Muscle fibres form by fusion of cells, so they are multinucleate and very long. The companion-cell link describes phloem sieve tubes.

items.stem: Which technique would best show where one specific protein is located inside a cell?
choices: Immunofluorescence, using antibodies tagged with a fluorescent marker
Freeze-fracture electron microscopy, splitting the membrane along its middle
Staining with iodine solution and viewing with a light microscope
Cryogenic electron microscopy of the whole tissue section
items.note: Fluorescent antibodies bind only to their target protein, so the glow shows its location. Freeze fracture shows membrane interiors; cryo-EM shows protein structure.

items.stem: Which of the following is a function of life that a unicellular organism such as Paramecium must carry out on its own?
choices: Formation of tissues from groups of similar cells working together
Transport of oxygen by a circulatory system to its organelles
Sexual reproduction only, since it cannot divide by mitosis
Excretion of metabolic waste such as ammonia across its membrane
items.note: Unicellular organisms perform all functions of life (homeostasis, metabolism, nutrition, movement, excretion, growth, response, reproduction) in one cell.

items.stem: The resolution of an electron microscope is much better than that of a light microscope because:
choices: Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than visible light
Electron microscopes use stronger glass lenses than light microscopes
Electrons can pass through thicker specimens than light can
Electron microscopes give higher magnification so detail is resolved
items.note: Resolution depends on wavelength: shorter wavelength separates closer points. Magnification alone does not add detail.

items.stem: Which evidence best supports the theory that mitochondria evolved by endosymbiosis?
choices: They are surrounded by a single membrane like the plasma membrane
They have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, like bacteria
They contain 80S ribosomes like those in the cytoplasm of eukaryotes
They are made by the Golgi apparatus whenever the cell needs energy
items.note: Mitochondria (and chloroplasts) have naked circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, a double membrane and divide by binary fission — all prokaryote features.

items.stem: All cells in a human body contain the same genes, yet a liver cell differs from a nerve cell. This is because:
choices: Each cell type loses the genes it does not need during development
Mutations in each cell type create the new genes it needs
Different genes are expressed in different cell types
Nerve cells have more chromosomes than liver cells
items.note: Differentiation results from differential gene expression; the genome is (almost always) the same in every body cell.

items.stem: Outline three differences between a prokaryotic cell and an animal cell.
markscheme: Prokaryote has no nucleus (DNA in nucleoid); animal cell has DNA in a nucleus (1)
Prokaryote DNA is circular and naked; animal DNA is linear with histones (1)
Prokaryote has 70S ribosomes; animal cell has 80S (1)
Prokaryote has a cell wall (peptidoglycan); animal cell has none (1)
Prokaryote lacks membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria (1)
items.tactic: Each difference must state both sides; "prokaryotes have no nucleus" alone is often only half a point.

items.stem: Explain why a large central vacuole is useful to a plant cell but would not be useful to an animal cell.
markscheme: Vacuole fills with water, pushing the membrane against the cell wall (1)
This generates turgor pressure that supports the plant (1)
Animal cells have no wall to resist the pressure, so they would burst / they rely on other support (1)
items.tactic: Explain = give the reason and the consequence; link structure to function.

items.stem: Outline the origin of eukaryotic cells by endosymbiosis.
markscheme: An ancestral cell engulfed an aerobic prokaryote by endocytosis (1)
The prokaryote was not digested and survived inside, giving a mutual benefit (1)
It became the mitochondrion, sharing its ATP with the host (1)
A later engulfment of a photosynthetic prokaryote gave chloroplasts in some lines (1)
items.tactic: Outline: a short sequence of events, in order.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) A student measured an invented single-celled organism under a light microscope. The eyepiece graticule was calibrated so that one eyepiece unit = 2.5 µm at ×400. The cell measured 32 eyepiece units long. A photo of the same cell, printed for her notes, was 64 mm long.
(a) Calculate the actual length of the cell. (b) Calculate the magnification of the printed photo. (c) State why the eyepiece graticule must be recalibrated if she switches to the ×100 objective.
markscheme: (c) Each eyepiece unit covers a different actual distance at a different magnification (the graticule scale stays the same while the image size changes) (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
